outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 proves or disproves that the primes of the form (k·b^n+c)/gcd(k+c,b−1) are infinite for any admissible (k,b,c). The in-window items are single primes for single triples (August 2024, April 2025), compositeness papers, Cullen-form results outside this family, and a 2025 thesis whose claimed extension to prime classifications I could not read in full.
problem_asks: (1) For every admissible triple (k, b, c): integers k ≥ 1, b ≥ 2, c ≠ 0, with gcd(k, c) = 1 and gcd(b, c) = 1. These are hypotheses on the triple, not conclusions. (2) For each such triple, the values (k·b^n + c)/gcd(k + c, b − 1) for integers n ≥ 1 are asked to include infinitely many primes. The divisor gcd(k + c, b − 1) depends only on the triple and the value increases strictly with n (since b ≥ 2), so infinitely many prime values is the same as infinitely many exponents n giving a prime. (3) The question is posed in universal form ('for any given ... are there infinitely many'), so the natural reading is one yes-or-no per admissible triple, with a counterexample being a triple having only finitely many such primes. The statement does not ask for a uniform answer over all triples in one argument, and it does not ask for any count, density, or particular exponent.

events.what_happened: Jon Grantham and Andrew Granville, 'Fibonacci primes, primes of the form 2^n−k and beyond' (arXiv:2307.07894). A heuristic conjecture for primes among terms of exponentially growing linear recurrences u_n: either only finitely many u_n are prime, or about c_u·log N of the u_n with n ≤ N are prime. The motivating families are primes 2^n−k with k odd, and more generally a·2^n+b with coprime odd a and b. The authors compare the conjecture with computed data. They prove no infinitude statement.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jul 2023 (the page says this draft was submitted in error); v2 18 Jul 2023; v3 9 Sep 2024 with minor changes matching the published version. Journal reference: J. Number Theory 261 (2024), 190–219.
events.delivers: Nothing proved. A conjecture: for u_n in the base-2 family a·2^n+b with a, b coprime and odd, and for exponentially growing linear recurrences in general, the dichotomy 'finitely many prime u_n' or 'about c·log N prime u_n up to N'. Scope against the bullet: at base b = 2 the bullet's expression is exactly k·2^n+c, and the paper's odd-a hypothesis is stronger than the bullet's (the bullet allows even k, requiring only gcd(k,c) = 1 with c odd). The paper's own examples are a·2^n+b, so the bullet's general-base case is outside what it treats.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The paper states a heuristic dichotomy and gives no proof that any admissible triple has infinitely many prime values, at base 2 or otherwise.

checked_by.who: Journal of Number Theory editorial and refereeing process
checked_by.qualification: A refereed number theory journal. The acceptance is a publication decision for a conjecture, not a verification of a proof.
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (J. Number Theory 261, 2024); the journal page itself was not opened, the reference is from the arXiv abstract page.

events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 3 months (15 Jul 2023 to Oct 2026)
events.direction: Gives the 'infinitely many' outcome (growth like c·log N) as one of two heuristic alternatives. It does not say which holds for any given triple. It is a prediction bearing on the bullet's question, not a result in either direction.

events.what_happened: Olli Järviniemi and Joni Teräväinen, 'Composite values of shifted exponentials' (arXiv:2010.01789; Adv. Math. 429 (2023) 109187). Conditional on GRH and a pair-correlation-type hypothesis, 2^n+5 is composite for almost all n (the open problem posed by Hooley, proposed by Kalai as a Polymath project). The methods give k-almost-primality on density-zero sets for a^n−b, and the abstract says a^p−b is composite for almost all primes p when (a,b) ≠ (2,1), without stating whether that last result is conditional. This is the composite direction, not infinitude of primes.
events.revisions: v1 5 Oct 2020; v2 19 Jun 2023 with referee comments incorporated; published Adv. Math. 429 (2023) 109187.
events.delivers: Conditional composite-value results for shifted exponentials a^n−b, for example 2^n+5 composite for almost all n. Scope against the bullet: the case k = 1, base a, c = −b with gcd(a, b) = 1 lies inside the bullet's admissible triples, and 2^n+5 is the triple (1, 2, 5). The result is for composites only, under GRH plus a pair-correlation-type hypothesis. It gives no unconditional statement about primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. A density-one set of composite terms is compatible with infinitely many primes, so the result does not decide infinitude.

checked_by.who: Adv. Math. editorial and refereeing process
checked_by.qualification: A refereed journal. The arXiv v2 notes that referee comments were incorporated.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published (Adv. Math. 429, 2023); the journal page was not opened, the reference is from the arXiv abstract page.

events.doubts: The main results are conditional on GRH plus pair correlation, or on a Brun–Titchmarsh-type inequality in number fields. The abstract does not say whether the a^p−b statement is conditional.
events.direction: Cuts toward composite values: for the shifted exponentials it covers, almost all terms are composite (conditionally). It does not answer the bullet's question either way.

events.what_happened: Michael Filaseta, Robert Groth and Thomas Luckner, 'Generalized Sierpiński Numbers' (arXiv:2305.09219). For a fixed integer A ≥ 2 there is an odd positive k such that k·a^n+1 is composite for every a in [2, A] and every n ≥ 1. Journal reference Colloquium Mathematicum 174 (2023) is from a search snippet; the publisher page was not opened.
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 16 May 2023 (per the arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A composite-for-all-n existence result for k·a^n+1, simultaneously over a range of bases. Scope against the bullet: this is the bullet's c = +1 family with the composite-for-all-n property. It gives no primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The result says some k yield no primes at all for the stated bases.

checked_by.who: Colloquium Mathematicum editorial and refereeing process
checked_by.qualification: A refereed journal, per the search snippet.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published (Colloq. Math. 174, 2023), journal reference taken from a search snippet.

events.direction: Composite direction: for the k it constructs, k·a^n+1 is never prime for the stated bases. Opposite to infinitude of primes for those k.
events.object: An odd k, not given explicitly in the abstract, with k·a^n+1 composite for all a in [2, A] and all n ≥ 1; the construction is an existence result.

events.what_happened: Robert S. Groth, 'Generalized Sierpiński Numbers and New Irreducibility Criteria on Legendre Polynomials', doctoral dissertation, University of South Carolina, advisor Michael Filaseta, date of award 30 April 2025 (scholarcommons.sc.edu/etd/8101). The abstract as I read it: for fixed R ≥ 1 and A ≥ 2 there are infinitely many odd k such that k·r·a^n+1 is composite for every r in [1, R], a in [2, A] and n ≥ 1; these k form congruence classes L mod M with gcd(L, M) = 1; and the work of J. Maynard and D. K. L. Shiu 'allow[s] us to extend these results to classifications of prime numbers'. The thesis PDF returned HTTP 403, so the content of the prime-classification extension is unknown to me.
events.delivers: On the abstract as read: composite-for-all-n existence results for k·r·a^n+1, the bullet's c = +1 case with a fixed multiplier r. The prime-classification extension is not specified in what I could read. If it asserts infinitely many primes of the form k·a^n+1 for a given k, it would bear on the bullet's c = +1 case. If it concerns runs of consecutive primes in arithmetic progressions (the Maynard and Shiu results the abstract cites, as summarised in search results), it would not bear on the bullet.
events.remains: On the abstract as read, all of problem_asks. The k-classes it describes are composite-producing, so any prime statement would have to be a separate claim, which I could not read.

checked_by.who: Robert S. Groth (author) and the University of South Carolina doctoral committee (advisor Michael Filaseta)
checked_by.qualification: A mathematics doctoral dissertation. The committee members were not identified and their review was not verified.
checked_by.what_they_did: Dissertation approved and awarded 30 April 2025 (per the repository record). No public review or verification of its prime-classification claim found.

events.doubts: The prime-classification claim appears only in the abstract I could read; the body was not readable. The Maynard and Shiu results cited (Maynard 2016 on dense clusters of primes in arithmetic progressions; Shiu 2000 on strings of consecutive primes in progressions) concern prime strings and do not by themselves yield infinitely many primes of exponential form. That reading is mine and not checked against the thesis.
events.direction: The composite-producing results cut against primality for the k they produce. The prime-classification claim is undetermined from what I could read.

events.what_happened: Riesel candidate elimination. Wikipedia's Riesel number page (opened) reports that the most recent elimination was in August 2024, when 107347 × 223427517 − 1 was found to be prime by Ryan Propper, with 7,052,391 digits. This removes k = 107347 from the candidate list below 509203 for the Riesel problem.
events.delivers: One prime of the form 107347·2^n − 1, at one exponent. The triple (107347, 2, −1) is admissible: gcd(107347, −1) = 1, gcd(2, −1) = 1, and the divisor gcd(107346, 1) = 1, so the bullet's expression is 107347·2^n − 1. It shows that this one triple has at least one prime value.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for this triple, including infinitude, which one prime does not touch.
events.directly_checkable: 107347·2^223427517 − 1 can be tested by any primality program. Not run here.
events.direction: A single prime for a single admissible triple. It is a finite instance of a question asking for infinitely many primes, so it does not move the bullet's question, and it cuts against no part of the bullet.
events.object: 107347·2^223427517 − 1, a 7,052,391-digit prime found by search. The primality test used is not stated in the page I read.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's Sierpiński/Riesel Base 5 project: on 8 April 2025, 67612·5^5501582 + 1 was found prime (Kai Presler), eliminating k = 67612 from the base-5 Sierpiński candidates. The prime has 3,845,446 digits, and a second machine confirmed it prime on 8 April 2025 (LLR2 per search-result text). The BOINC-AF announcement and the Prime-Wiki entry could not be opened (DNS failure; HTTP 503), so these details come from search-result text only.
events.delivers: One prime of the form 67612·5^n + 1, at one exponent. The triple (67612, 5, +1) is admissible: gcd(67612, 1) = 1, gcd(5, 1) = 1, and the divisor gcd(67613, 4) = 1. It shows at least one prime value for this triple, and nothing about infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for this triple.
events.directly_checkable: 67612·5^5501582 + 1 can be tested by a primality program. Not run here.
events.direction: A single prime for one Sierpiński candidate, which removes k = 67612 from the composite-for-all-n candidate set. It says nothing about infinitude for that triple.
events.object: 67612·5^5501582 + 1, a 3,845,446-digit prime from the PrimeGrid base-5 search (per search-result text, not opened).

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's Generalized Cullen/Woodall search found 4052186·69^4052186 + 1 on 16 April 2025, listed as the largest known generalized Cullen prime. The Prime Pages Top 20 (opened) lists it at rank 1 with 7,451,366 digits and discoverer code A61. Search text credits Mark Williams. Confirmed prime 17 April 2025. Wikipedia's Cullen number article (opened) gives the same figure as of April 2025.
events.delivers: One prime of the form n·69^n + 1. The multiplier is the exponent n, not a fixed k, so this is outside the bullet's form k·b^n+c. It shows a prime in a neighbouring family and nothing about the bullet's question.
events.directly_checkable: 4052186·69^4052186 + 1 can be tested by a primality program. Not run here.
events.direction: No bearing on the bullet: it is a prime in a family whose multiplier grows with the exponent.

events.what_happened: Hailey Evans, Joshua Harrington, Kendall Heiney, Maggie Wieczorek, 'Generalized Sierpiński and Riesel numbers of the form tb^t+α' (arXiv:2508.05942). Shows infinitely many b-Sierpiński and b-Riesel numbers of the form tb^t+α for any nonzero integer α, and infinitely many b-Brier numbers of that form when b+1 is not a power of 2.
events.revisions: v1 8 Aug 2025 only, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Composite-for-all-n results on k·b^n ± 1 for k in a family with the multiplier t tied to the exponent, so the family is not the bullet's k·b^n+c with fixed k. It proves no primality statement.
events.direction: Composite direction, and outside the bullet's form because the coefficient of b^n is tied to the exponent.

events.what_happened: Chris Bispels, Matthew Cohen, Joshua Harrington, Joshua Lowrance, Kaelyn Pontes, Leif Schaumann, Tony W. H. Wong, 'On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers' (arXiv:2505.00778). Asks whether b-repdigits and b-repunits occur among Sierpiński and Riesel numbers, defined by composite-for-all-n for k·2^n ± 1. Journal reference INTEGERS 26 (2026) A12.
events.revisions: v1 1 May 2025; v2 24 Jul 2025; journal reference INTEGERS 26 (2026) A12 (journal date from a Zenodo search snippet, not opened).
events.delivers: Compositeness results on repdigit and repunit members of Sierpiński and Riesel sets. The definitions given are for base 2. A search snippet describes an infinitude statement for base b, which the abstract page did not show, so I do not record it as established.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published (INTEGERS 26, 2026, A12), per the arXiv journal reference.

events.direction: Composite direction, and about base-2 definitions. It does not bear on infinitude of primes.

events.what_happened: Andrew Granville and Francesco Pappalardi, 'Two dimensional covering systems and possible prime producing a^m − b^n' (arXiv:2601.10296). Uses two-dimensional covering systems to find pairs (a, b) for which a^m − b^n always has a prime divisor from a fixed finite set, and conjectures the only possible obstructions to |a^m − b^n| taking infinitely many distinct prime values. v2 (11 Apr 2026) corrects a mistake a referee found.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jan 2026; v2 11 Apr 2026, correcting a mistake a referee found.
events.delivers: For suitable pairs (a, b), a fixed finite set of primes divides a^m − b^n for all m and n. A fixed prime divisor of every term leaves only terms equal to those primes as possible prime values, so the result is an obstruction-type statement for those pairs. The paper also conjectures the full obstruction set. Scope: two-variable exponential differences, not a single exponential k·b^n+c with fixed k, b, c.

checked_by.what_they_did: Revised v2 after a referee found an error in v1. No independent verification found.

events.doubts: The v1 error a referee found is recorded as corrected in v2. The v2 correction is not described in the abstract page I read.
events.direction: Obstruction-type for the pairs it covers, in a different question (two-variable differences). Not a statement about the bullet's family.

events.what_happened: Paulius Virbalas, 'On the generalized Sierpiński and Riesel numbers' (arXiv:2610.05149; first submitted 4 Oct 2026; the page says it is published in Boletín de Matemáticas). For any base b ≥ 2 it constructs an infinite arithmetic progression of k that are both generalized Sierpiński and generalized Riesel numbers in base b, using covering systems and Zsigmondy's theorem: each of k·b^n ± 1 has at least two distinct prime factors.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Composite-for-all-n results for k·b^n ± 1 on an arithmetic progression of k, for every base. Scope: the bullet's c = ±1 case with fixed k; the bullet asks for infinitely many primes, and this result shows the terms have composite values for all n on that progression.
events.direction: Composite direction: for the k on the progression, no term is prime. Opposite to infinitude of primes for those k.
events.object: An infinite arithmetic progression of k, such that for each k and each n both k·b^n+1 and k·b^n−1 are composite, from a covering-system argument (existence, not an explicit list).

events.what_happened: Vikas Godara and Divyum Sharma, 'Additive Diophantine Equations involving S-Units, Factorials and Ternary Recurrences with repeated root' (arXiv:2605.28449, first submitted 27 May 2026). Shows that the greatest prime divisor of Cullen numbers n·2^n+1 minus bounded combinations of factorials tends to infinity, effectively, and solves C_n = m1! + m2! + s for s with prime factors only 2, 3, 5, 7.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Results on the size of the greatest prime divisor and on a Diophantine equation for Cullen numbers. Scope: Cullen numbers have the exponent as the multiplier, so they are outside the bullet's k·b^n+c form. It says nothing about infinitely many Cullen primes.
events.direction: No bearing on infinitude of primes in the bullet's family.

events.what_happened: Herbert Batte, Eric F. Bravo, Florian Luca, 'Cullen and Woodall numbers in Padovan and Perrin sequences' (arXiv:2605.23084, first submitted 21 May 2026). Determines which Woodall numbers m·2^m−1 lie in the Padovan sequence (only 1 and 7) and which Cullen numbers lie in the Perrin sequence (only 3).
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Membership of Cullen and Woodall numbers in two recurrence sequences. Scope: outside the bullet's form (multiplier tied to the exponent), and about membership, not primality. Says nothing on whether Cullen or Woodall numbers are prime.
events.direction: No bearing on the bullet's question.

summary: Searched 49 web queries (listed verbatim below), plus three arXiv listing searches and one zbMATH search (HTTP 403). I opened the live Wikipedia list (read through a summarising fetch; the bullet's text and absence of any solved marker were taken from that summary, not verbatim), and the frozen page locally, where the bullet appears at line 605 of the prime-numbers list with no citation. Its origin is not established: searches for Dubner, Ribenboim, Guy and the gcd(k+c, b−1) form returned nothing that states it. The nearest sources are the Riesel and Sierpiński families normalised by gcd(k±1, b−1) (Wikipedia's Riesel number page explains that the gcd is a trivial factor shared by every term), Dubner's generalized Cullen family n·b^n+1, and Grantham and Granville's 2023 heuristic for a·2^n+b. Nothing in the window proves or disproves infinitude of primes for any admissible triple, and nothing moves the question: the in-window items are single primes for single triples (Riesel k = 107347 with base 2 and c = −1, August 2024, per Wikipedia; Sierpiński k = 67612 with base 5 and c = +1, 8 April 2025, per search text only), composite-direction results (Evans et al. 2025; Bispels et al. 2025; Virbalas 2026), and Cullen-form results outside the bullet's form (the April 2025 generalized Cullen prime 4052186·69^n+1; Godara and Sharma 2026; Batte, Bravo and Luca 2026). Close calls: (a) Groth's 2025 thesis abstract says the Maynard and Shiu results extend its k-results to 'classifications of prime numbers'. If that means infinitely many primes of the form k·a^n+1 for a fixed k, it would be an in-scope event with class-level content, and I could not read the thesis to decide (HTTP 403), so I record it as unresolved rather than as a non-event. (b) The single-prime eliminations are finite instances for one triple each, so I treat them as not bearing on infinitude, which is the §2.1 reading; a reader who counted them would still have no class-level theorem. (c) Grantham and Granville's heuristic predicts the infinitely-many branch as one of two possibilities for base-2 families of this shape. It is a conjecture and does not settle any triple. Two items are noted in passing and are not events: a search summary says Grantham–Granville is cited in an OEIS comment (2^k−5 primes), which I did not open; and Montaron's 2020 'Exponential prime sequences' (arXiv:2011.14653, opened) uses exponents n^d, a different family, conditional on Cramér's conjecture. AI: no AI system is credited with any result on this bullet, so ai.none_found is true for every event. I ran explicit AI searches on the problem's own family (Cullen, Woodall, Riesel, Sierpiński, generalized Cullen, Lean formalisations, covering systems, AlphaEvolve, Gemini and AlphaProof, GPT-5.5 and 5.6, and Claude), none of which turned up a related result. The AI prime claims that did appear all concern prime gaps, not this family: OpenAI's Lean-verified bounded prime gap of 186 (one aggregator source, not checked against a primary source); Axiom's Lean verification of the 246 bounded-gap theorem (a formalisation of a known result, August 2026); and GPT-5.6 prime-gap claims of September 2026, which the sources I found contradict on the model and team and which could not be verified. AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763, 9 of 353 Erdős problems, 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures) and OEIS Open (arXiv:2608.11941, 147 of 492 by language models) list no item I could identify as belonging to this family from their abstracts; I did not enumerate the OEIS items. A Scientific American piece on an Anthropic paper about prime distribution linked to the Riemann hypothesis concerns a different question, and I did not confirm its date.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the record differently is Groth's 2025 thesis: if its Maynard–Shiu extension to prime classifications is a theorem that infinitely many primes of the form k·a^n+1 occur for some class of k, then it would be an in-scope event that partly answers the bullet for the c = +1 case, and the record's 'nothing moves the question' reading would be wrong. A second reading treats the single-prime eliminations as instances that count toward a class-level claim, though §2.1 says finitely many instances of a universal claim move nothing. A third reading takes the Grantham–Granville heuristic as evidence that the expected answer to the bullet is 'infinitely many' for base-2 families with coprime odd entries. That is a reading of expectation, not of settled status.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Groth's 2025 thesis (scholarcommons.sc.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=9006&context=etd, which returned HTTP 403 to my fetcher): the theorem behind 'classifications of prime numbers', its hypotheses on k and a, and whether it asserts infinitely many primes of the form k·a^n+1 for fixed k or only classes of composite values. (2) The PrimeGrid and Prime-Wiki records for Riesel 107347 (August 2024) and Sierpiński base-5 k = 67612 (April 2025), which I could not reach (boinc-af.org did not resolve; rieselprime.de returned 503), and which would confirm the date and discoverer. (3) The origin of the gcd(k+c, b−1) bullet: the Wikipedia edit history or the source it was taken from, which would fix the conjecture's intended scope. (4) An enumeration of the OEIS Open and AlphaProof Nexus OEIS results, and of the formal-conjectures repository, for any sequence in this family. (5) A working zbMATH search for 2024–2026 journal papers on Riesel, Sierpiński, Cullen or Woodall primality.

event.what_happened: Robert S. Groth, 'Generalized Sierpiński Numbers and New Irreducibility Criteria on Legendre Polynomials', doctoral dissertation, University of South Carolina, advisor Michael Filaseta, date of award 30 April 2025 (scholarcommons.sc.edu/etd/8101). The abstract as I read it: for fixed R ≥ 1 and A ≥ 2 there are infinitely many odd k such that k·r·a^n+1 is composite for every r in [1, R], a in [2, A] and n ≥ 1; these k form congruence classes L mod M with gcd(L, M) = 1; and the work of J. Maynard and D. K. L. Shiu 'allow[s] us to extend these results to classifications of prime numbers'. The thesis PDF returned HTTP 403, so the content of the prime-classification extension is unknown to me.
event.delivers: On the abstract as read: composite-for-all-n existence results for k·r·a^n+1, the bullet's c = +1 case with a fixed multiplier r. The prime-classification extension is not specified in what I could read. If it asserts infinitely many primes of the form k·a^n+1 for a given k, it would bear on the bullet's c = +1 case. If it concerns runs of consecutive primes in arithmetic progressions (the Maynard and Shiu results the abstract cites, as summarised in search results), it would not bear on the bullet.
event.remains: On the abstract as read, all of problem_asks. The k-classes it describes are composite-producing, so any prime statement would have to be a separate claim, which I could not read.

checked_by.who: Robert S. Groth (author) and the University of South Carolina doctoral committee (advisor Michael Filaseta)
checked_by.qualification: A mathematics doctoral dissertation. The committee members were not identified and their review was not verified.
checked_by.what_they_did: Dissertation approved and awarded 30 April 2025 (per the repository record). No public review or verification of its prime-classification claim found.

event.doubts: The prime-classification claim appears only in the abstract I could read; the body was not readable. The Maynard and Shiu results cited (Maynard 2016 on dense clusters of primes in arithmetic progressions; Shiu 2000 on strings of consecutive primes in progressions) concern prime strings and do not by themselves yield infinitely many primes of exponential form. That reading is mine and not checked against the thesis.
event.direction: The composite-producing results cut against primality for the k they produce. The prime-classification claim is undetermined from what I could read.

events.credibility_reason: Only the abstract was readable; the content of the claimed 'prime classification' extension is unknown, so what the thesis actually establishes beyond composite-producing k-classes cannot be confirmed.

judgement.why: Read literally, the statement asks whether every admissible triple yields infinitely many primes, and it already fails before the snapshot: classical Sierpiński/Riesel numbers (e.g. k·2^n+1 with a covering set, divisor gcd(k+1,1)=1) are admissible triples with no prime values at all. Composite-for-all-n results on fixed k (Filaseta–Groth–Luckner, Groth's thesis, Evans et al. where the k are fixed numbers of the form tb^t+α, Bispels et al., Virbalas) therefore exhibit further counterexample triples for a claim already known to fail; per F4 these move the frontier rather than settle anything, so I scored them bound with null direction while recording the objects as counterexamples. Single record primes are instances. Cullen-form results (multiplier tied to exponent), two-variable a^m−b^n, and the conditional almost-all-composite result are variants. Grantham–Granville is a heuristic: none. No AI involvement anywhere. Groth's thesis counts as digested via committee approval (F9), but its unread prime-classification claim makes it doubtful.
judgement.doubts: The close call is the composite-family events: they could alternatively be read as 'case' (settling specific triples negatively, direction refuted), which would give a misleading 'partial, refuted' status dated 2025–26 for a statement literally refuted decades earlier; or as 'none' if the list item implicitly excludes covering-set triples. The researcher read Evans et al. as outside the form, but the Sierpiński/Riesel numbers there are fixed k values, so I treated it as in-family. The literal statement's falsity rests on classical Sierpiński numbers not recorded as events, so open_stale is not available from the record.
